title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Dust and the Dead—Dickens's London of Waste and Worth

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close reading of Charles Dickens's last completed novel, and perhaps his greatest.
I'm your host, and over this series we'll be moving through the novel passage by passage — its darkness, its comedy, its astonishing range of human life.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel about London as a great system of waste — dust-heaps, river mud, social refuse — and about who gets to be counted as a human being within that system.
Three extraordinary readers join me today, and I want to introduce them properly.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — he will not let us look away from what the system produces.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads for moral imagination — for character tested by circumstance, for individual goodness and its costs.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and devoted re-reader of this novel, who comes to it for the verbal music, the comedy, the moments that make you stop on a sentence and stay there.
Today's opening asks: what kind of world does Dickens give us from the very first pages of this novel — and what kind of vision does he sustain to its very last?
What strikes me, returning to this novel again, is how consistently Dickens uses atmosphere not as decoration but as moral verdict.
Take the passage where Bradley Headstone creeps up the dark staircase toward Wrayburn's chambers.
Dickens writes: 'The haggard head floated up the dark staircase, and softly descended nearer to the floor outside the outer door of the chambers.'
That phrase — 'the haggard head' — is doing something precise and disturbing.
Bradley Headstone has been reduced, in this moment, to a disembodied instrument of obsession — not a man but a function.
And what the novel makes clear is that the system that produced Bradley — the respectable working man straining to be middle-class — has consumed him entirely from within.
Then Dickens administers a final quiet sting, telling us:

'If Lightwood could have seen the face which kept him awake, staring and listening in the darkness outside the door as he spoke of it, he might have been less disposed to sleep, through the remainder of the night.'
That's Gothic machinery, yes — but it is also a precise map of class anxiety and suppressed violence.
Daniel is right that the atmosphere is doing moral work — though I would frame it differently.
Bradley Headstone is not primarily a symptom of a system — he is a man who has chosen, fatally, to let passion overwhelm character.
That is a very old story, and Dickens tells it with Gothic relish, certainly — but the moral engine is Aristotelian, not Marxist.
Now — if one wants a passage that shows Dickens's atmosphere at its most precise and, I think, its most devastating — consider the Lammles.
Dickens gives them this exit:
'They walked arm-in-arm, showily enough, but without appearing to interchange a syllable.'
That is a marriage depicted with consummate economy — all the form of union, and none of the substance.
And then Dickens dismisses them with a sentence of almost casual finality.
'In turning the street corner they might have turned out of this world, for anything Mr and Mrs Boffin ever saw of them to the contrary.'
That is Dickens at his most chilling — not melodrama, but erasure.
What Edmund has just read aloud — 'they might have turned out of this world' — that is one of the sentences I return to most often in this novel.
Because it sounds almost gentle, and it is in fact a kind of damnation.
But I want to bring us somewhere entirely different — because this novel can do that, can move from the Gothic to the tender in a single chapter.
There is a scene between Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren — the dolls' dressmaker — that I think is one of the most quietly beautiful things Dickens ever wrote.
Lizzie is brushing out Jenny's long fair hair, and Dickens describes it like this:
'It fell in a beautiful shower over the poor shoulders that were much in need of such adorning rain.'
The word 'rain' there — not just metaphor, but blessing.

The 'poor shoulders' tell you everything about Jenny's physical suffering, and the hair becomes a kind of grace bestowed — freely, tenderly, between two women who have very little else to give each other.
That scene exists in the same novel as Bradley Headstone floating up a dark staircase, and that range is what makes Our Mutual Friend so remarkable.
Caroline puts her finger on something I think is essential — the tenderness between Lizzie and Jenny is not incidental to the novel's social argument, it is central to it.
These are two young women whom the world has used badly — one scarred by poverty and physical frailty, the other dragged up from the river's edge.
What they create for each other — that firelit intimacy, the hair, the shared gaze — is a counter-economy.
A form of value that the novel's official markets — the dust-heaps, the marriage market, the money-lending — cannot measure and do not reward.
Dickens is a more radical novelist than he sometimes gets credit for — and that scene is evidence.
I would not quarrel with 'radical' if we mean something like moral courage — the courage to see what is genuinely good and genuinely corrupt in the people before him.
The Lammles are corrupt in the way that truly worries Dickens — not because they are poor, but because they are hollow.
'Haggardly weary of one another, of themselves, and of all this world' — Dickens's own words, and they are not an economic indictment but a spiritual one.
That, I think, is where this novel lives — in the question of what a human soul is finally made of.
A question about souls — and about the systems that shape or break them.
That tension — between what society makes of us and what we make of ourselves — runs through every chapter of this novel.

And it is precisely that tension we'll be tracing in the segments ahead — from the riverside to the drawing room, from the dust-heap to the firelit attic where two women share something the market cannot name.

segments.title: Bella's Mercy: How a Woman Learns to Love without Money

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — as seriously as it deserves.
I'm your host, and today we're focusing on one of the novel's most surprisingly modern achievements: the transformation of Bella Wilfer.
Bella begins the novel as a young woman who is frankly, cheerfully mercenary — money is her stated ambition and she doesn't apologise for it.
By the end, something profound has shifted — but how, and at what cost?
With me today are three readers who each bring a sharply different eye to this question.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as maps of class power — and he'll want to ask who exactly benefits from Bella's change of heart.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes moral imagination is the true engine of great fiction — and he has strong views on what Bella's story is really about.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has re-read this novel many times and has a particular affection for Bella as a character.
Let's begin where Bella herself begins: with money, and the voice that tells her to go in for it.
The passage I keep returning to is Mr Boffin's speech — the moment he lays out his philosophy for Bella with such relish.
He doesn't just advise her — he celebrates the advice, rolls it around in his mouth.
Listen to how Dickens writes it:
'Go in for money, my love. Money's the article. You'll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you'll live and die rich.'
And then that final flourish — 'R—r—rich!' — with the stutter of pure appetite.
There's something almost hypnotic about it — the word 'money' repeated like a spell being cast over her.
And notice what Boffin is actually doing there — he's not corrupting Bella from innocence.
He's giving her a language for something she already believes — he's the system speaking through a friendly face.
That's precisely what makes Bella's reaction in her room so charged.
She can't dismiss what he said because it IS what she says to herself.
Dickens gives her this extraordinary interior monologue — she interrogates herself in the looking-glass:

'What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it.'
The logic traps her — she can't refute it, she can only feel its wrongness.
That is ideological dissonance, rendered as comedy — and it is very precise writing.
I wouldn't use the word 'ideological,' but I'll grant you the precision.
What Dickens is doing in that scene is something far older than ideology — it is conscience asserting itself against appetite.
The looking-glass is not a Marxist symbol — it is the oldest device in moral fiction.
You look at yourself and you are required to ask: who are you, really?
And Dickens's great insight is that Bella asks it herself — with perfect contempt:
'Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?'
It is a magnificent sentence — comic and fierce and deeply self-aware all at once.
That is Bella beginning to become Bella — not through any external agency, but through the force of her own character.
And there's a moment with Lizzie Hexam that I think is the real hinge of the transformation — the scene where Bella literally punishes herself.
Lizzie's selflessness puts Bella's mercenary values into such sharp relief that she can't avoid seeing them.
Dickens writes it as comedy, but it's comedy with a real sting:
'There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of your self?'
And then she gives herself — Dickens actually writes this — a penitential poke in the side.
It's absurd and it's touching and it's Dickens at his most characteristic — making you laugh and wince at exactly the same moment.
That scene with Lizzie is important to me for a different reason.
It's Lizzie who holds the novel's truest moral position — and she's a working-class woman with no social power whatsoever.
When she describes what Eugene Wrayburn's gaze means to her — a man who can offer her nothing safe — she says something extraordinary:
'I would not have the light of them taken out of my life, for anything my life can give me.'
That is not sentiment — that is a woman refusing to price her own feelings.
Bella encounters in Lizzie the living refutation of Boffin's gospel — and she feels it before she can articulate it.
That is how Dickens does the work — not through argument, but through encounter.
I think Daniel has identified something important there, even if I'd frame it differently.
Lizzie is not simply a social symbol — she is a portrait of a particular kind of human greatness.
And what's striking is the tenderness with which the passage closes — Lizzie's confession to Bella is itself a kind of gift.
'I had no thought of ever parting with a single word of it, a moment before you came in; but you came in, and my mind changed.'
Trust given unexpectedly — that is what begins to dissolve Bella's armour.
There's another figure I want to draw into this conversation — one we haven't named yet.
Rokesmith — who watches all of this from a distance, literally from doorways.
There's a passage where he watches Betty Higden leave and Bella stand alone — and the prose is strangely, almost unbearably quiet.
Caroline, I wonder if you'd read it for us.
Yes — this is one of those sentences that Dickens builds and builds and then lets fall into complete stillness.

'The Secretary looked on from a doorway at the boofer lady thus encircled, and still looked on at the boofer lady standing alone there, when the determined old figure with its steady bright eyes was trudging through the streets, away from paralysis and pauperism.'
That word 'still' is doing so much work — he looks on and still looks on.
He cannot look away from her.
And then Betty Higden, with her 'steady bright eyes,' trudging away — from paralysis and pauperism.
Two worlds held in a single sentence — the man in love who cannot declare it, and the old woman choosing death on her own terms.
I'm glad you read that, because I think it's easy to miss how much the novel asks us to hold at once in that image.
Betty Higden is fleeing the workhouse — 'away from paralysis and pauperism' — choosing the open road and probable death over institutional charity.
And in the same moment, we see Rokesmith watching Bella — the love plot and the survival plot occupying the exact same frame.
That juxtaposition is not accidental — it is Dickens insisting that these stories belong together.
And what of Boffin himself — the 'dark cloud' that Bella sees?
The passage is Gothic in its simplicity:
'A dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit, overshadowing the once open face.'
Those three nouns — suspicion, covetousness, conceit — are the three sins of the miser, ranked with real precision.
And the phrase 'once open face' carries the whole weight of loss — the reader mourns something they loved before knowing they'd lost it.
Bella watching that change is the moral education of the novel in miniature.
What strikes me, listening to all of this, is how much of Bella's transformation is witnessed rather than willed.
She watches Boffin change, she listens to Lizzie, she stands alone while Rokesmith watches her.
The novel seems to be saying that moral change begins in attention — in the capacity to really see what's in front of you.
That's a question we'll carry into the rest of the episode — and I suspect our three guests won't all agree on what Dickens finally makes of it.

segments.title: The Joker and the Scheme: Harmon's Masquerade and the Plot's Engine

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We are deep into the machinery of this extraordinary novel, and today we are pulling apart one of its most intricate mechanisms: John Harmon's masquerade.
The disguise that drives the plot, the will buried in the Mound, the patient deception of a villain — all of it converging in one of the most satisfying confrontations in Victorian fiction.
With me are Dr. Daniel Rosen, who will want to know what this plot machinery is actually doing in terms of power and property.
Sir Edmund Leigh, who I suspect will have something precise and possibly withering to say about the question of character and justice.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt, who I know loves the passages where Dickens allows himself to be absolutely furious on behalf of his hero.
Let us begin with the roots of the plot — the Boffins, and what they were prepared to do for a boy the old miser was determined to destroy.
What always catches me about the Boffins is that their goodness is not serene.
It is hard-won, tested, physical — they have literally taken blows on behalf of John Harmon.
And Boffin recounts all of this to Mortimer Lightwood in this wonderful, blundering, entirely unself-congratulatory way.
He describes standing up for the boy time and again, being called every name Old Harmon could lay his tongue to.
And then this extraordinary image — Dickens gives us Old Harmon's cruelty through one unforgettable detail.

'I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet (she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head), and send it spinning across the yard.'

'And once, when he did this in a manner that amounted to personal, I should have given him a rattler for himself, if Mrs Boffin hadn't thrown herself betwixt us, and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.'
That repeated word — 'Dropped her' — is everything.
It is grief and shock and outrage compressed into two words, and Boffin's voice breaks under its own plainness.
Caroline is quite right to stress the physicality of it, though I would add: Dickens is also doing something rather classical here.
The Boffins are not given to eloquent moral pronouncements about John Harmon's situation.
They demonstrate their virtue through action and through suffering — which is, I think, the only reliable demonstration.
What is also notable is that Boffin makes no great claim for himself in the telling.
He says, in effect: we tried, we were knocked back, and still we tried again.
That is moral character in its proper sense — not sentiment, but persistence.
I don't want to deflect from what is genuinely moving here, because it is moving.
But I think Dickens is also showing us something structural: the cruelty of the old miser is not temperamental, it's proprietary.
Old Harmon treats human beings — his son, Mrs Boffin, even the bonnet — as objects he can hurl across a yard.
He is the logic of accumulation made flesh.
And what Boffin describes is really a sustained act of class resistance — two servants who refuse to accept that the master's authority extends to the destruction of a child.
The bonnet spinning across the yard is the image of that system at its most naked.
And yet, for all his cruelty, the old man does eventually — in a perverse, incomplete way — try to do right by the son he tormented.
Which brings us to Mrs Boffin's extraordinary response to inheriting the fortune — this proposal to find an orphan and give him John Harmon's name.
This is the passage that breaks me a little, every time.
Mrs Boffin has this great fortune, which has come to her through a kind of catastrophe — the death of the very boy she loved.
And her response is not to celebrate or to mourn in private, but to find a way to keep the name alive.
She says — and she says it with that characteristic Dickensian diffidence, as though she might be talked out of it —
'Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him.'
'Somehow, it would make me easier, I fancy. Say it's only a whim—'
That trailing dash after 'whim' — she is almost apologising for her own goodness.
Dickens understands that genuinely generous people are often embarrassed by their own impulses.
Caroline touches on something I find consistently admirable about Dickens's method with the Boffins.
He protects their goodness from self-satisfaction.
They are good the way simple people are good in the best moral literature — not through reasoning, but through instinct.
The proposal to adopt a child and name him John Harmon is not a programme; it is an act of piety toward the dead.
Burke would have recognised that impulse — the living obligated to the dead, memory as a kind of moral inheritance.
The instinct is real and beautiful, Edmund, I won't dispute that.
But notice what Dickens is also doing structurally: he is setting up the conditions for John Harmon to be recognised.
The Boffins' grief is not merely private sentiment — it is the mechanism by which the inheritance finds its rightful channel.
The fortune cannot be detached from the question of who deserves it — and Dickens won't let it be.
Which makes the confrontation with Wegg in the final movement so satisfying — because all of this accumulated moral weight crashes down on one spectacularly deserving target.
The Dutch bottle, the buried will, the long surveillance — let us talk about how Dickens choreographs that reckoning.
The Dutch bottle sequence is one of the great moments in the novel's plot architecture, and I want to be clear about why.
Old Harmon buried a will in the Mound — his own estate, built on refuse — that would have cast a slur on his children's memory.
Boffin finds it, is distressed by it, and buries it again — not to profit, but to protect two dead children.
And Harmon explains all of this to Wegg in terms that are scorching and precise.
'That Dutch bottle, scoundrel, contained the latest will of the many wills made by my unhappy self-tormenting father.'
'That will gives everything absolutely to my noble benefactor and yours, Mr Boffin, excluding and reviling me, and my sister (then already dead of a broken heart), by name.'
The anaphora — 'That Dutch bottle... that will... that Dutch bottle' — is not accidental.
It is the rhetoric of accusation, of reckoning — each repetition tightening the noose around Wegg's pretensions.
And before the legal exposition, there is that raw, unguarded moment where Harmon simply loses patience with Wegg as a human being.
He is knocking Wegg's head against the wall — literally — and he says, with what I can only describe as a kind of wistful fury:
'and I'd give a thousand pounds for leave to knock your brains out.'
It is almost comic — the very polished formulation of the wish to do violence.
Harmon is a man who has spent this entire novel suppressing himself, and in this moment the suppression cracks — but even the crack is controlled.
Dickens gives us his hero's fury in perfectly calibrated prose.
I think Caroline is identifying something that goes to the heart of Harmon as a character.
He has passed most of the novel under an assumed name, suppressing his own identity and his own rights, and for what?
To prove that the woman he might love could love a man, not a fortune.
That is a test of exceptional moral seriousness — and it costs him terribly.
So when the restraint finally breaks, even partially, we feel the accumulated weight of everything he has withheld.
Edmund makes a fair point about the personal cost, though I'd locate the drama slightly differently.
What strikes me about the Wegg sequence is that it is simultaneously a personal unmasking and a legal settlement.
And Harmon is explicit that the deception was sustained deliberately — not just discovered after the fact.
He tells Wegg exactly what was done to him, and why, and he is honest that he wanted the maximum possible disappointment.
'I kept you under good observation from my first appearance here, and though Sloppy has long made it the chief occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow.'
The phrase 'chief occupation and delight' is perfect — Sloppy's guileless devotion weaponised against a man who never noticed him.
And then: 'in order that your disappointment might be the heaviest possible disappointment.'
There is no attempt to dress that up as anything other than what it is — a satisfaction, and a just one.
And that is what makes the Wegg scenes so unusual in the novel's moral landscape.
Dickens generally insists on a kind of redemptive mercy — characters are given exits, softened endings.
But Wegg is given none of that.
He is humiliated as thoroughly and publicly as Dickens can manage, and the novel seems to enjoy it.
Which tells us something about how seriously the novel takes the crime of exploiting the Boffins' goodness.
That's a sharp observation to close on — the punishment calibrated to the crime, and the crime being not theft but the betrayal of genuine decency.
The masquerade at the heart of this novel is not just a plot device — it is Dickens asking who we really are when the inheritance is stripped away.
We'll take that question into our next segment, where we consider what the novel does with the idea of identity under assumed names — and what it costs to finally come home to yourself.

segments.title: Rogue Riches and Respectability: Boffin's Corruption and Dickens's Satire

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we are deep in the money, the mud, and the magnificent absurdity of Dickens's Golden Dustman.
Nicodemus Boffin — a man who inherits a fortune built on refuse — becomes the novel's great satirical lens on wealth, respectability, and the parasites they attract.
With me today are three readers who know this novel with extraordinary intimacy.
Dr. Daniel Rosen reads Dickens as a radical anatomist of class power — the institutions, the charities, the aristocracy — all mechanisms of extraction.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the Oxford don's eye for moral character — for what wealth does to individual souls, not just to social structures.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt, who has been reading and re-reading this novel since she was a teenager, and who hears the music in every sentence.
Let us begin with the mansion — that eminently aristocratic family mansion — and what it tells us about Boffin's new world.
The moment Dickens introduces us to Boffin in that mansion, he does something quietly devastating.
He calls him — with that perfectly calibrated sneer — 'the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour.'
'The minion of fortune and the worm of the hour.'
And then he immediately softens it — 'or in less cutting language, Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire.'
That comic gear-shift — the narrator pretending to be kinder than he just was — is pure Dickens.
But then comes the image I keep returning to.
'Like an eminently aristocratic family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite amount of parasites.'
An aristocratic family cheese — I defy anyone to improve on that as a description of inherited wealth.
Caroline is right to linger on that image, and I don't think one should hurry past what Dickens is also doing to Boffin himself.
The man is not destroyed by the mansion — he is merely resigned to it, because Mrs Boffin enjoys herself completely and Bella is delighted.
Boffin's goodness — his fundamental, stubborn goodness — is what makes the satire sting.
He regards the parasites as a sort of perpetual Legacy Duty and moves on.
There is something almost Johnsonian in that — the wise man accepts the inconveniences of his station without complaint.
Dickens is a moralist, always — and the moral here is that wealth tests character, but character can endure.
I want to press on the word 'parasites,' because Dickens is not using it casually.
What follows in the next chapters is a systematic catalogue — the Secretary reading the letters — and it is one of the most ferocious passages of social comedy in the novel.
Look at what Dickens does with the Duke of Linseed.
The letter begins with all the warmth of personal address, and then the narrator adds the kicker:
'only lithographed by the hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand.'
The aristocracy does not even bother to write its own begging letters.
They outsource the performance of personal connection to the printing press — and then have the grace to add the fee in a postscript.
That postscript — three guineas! — is one of the great comic details.
But what I love about that whole passage is the rhythm of accumulation.
Fifty-seven churches, forty-two parsonage houses, seven-and-twenty organs, twelve hundred children.
Dickens is doing something almost liturgical — the repetition builds and builds until it collapses under its own absurdity.
Then we move to the individual beggars in the next section, and the register shifts — funnier, sharper, almost unbearably precise.
The line that stops me every time is about the documents they enclose.
'They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf.'
Minced veal to a calf — it is grotesque and hilarious and somehow also slightly tragic all at once.
The comic taxonomy of beggars in that passage is superb — one must give Dickens his full due there.
The daughters of general officers, 'long accustomed to every luxury of life, except spelling' — that parenthesis alone is worth several pages of social analysis.
But I think Daniel and Caroline are both in danger of reading the satire as purely political — as though Dickens were simply prosecuting the rich.
The inspired beggar sitting by his guttering candle when an angel whispers Boffin's name — that figure is comic, yes.
But Dickens also makes him pitiable — a cold potato and water by a lucifer-match.
The satire is in the pretension, not in the need.
Edmund, I think you're making an important distinction and I actually agree with it — to a point.
But the pretension itself is a product of the system.

The nobly independent beggar who regards gold as dross — that magnificent performance of contempt for money while desperately soliciting it — is a character produced by a culture that treats wealth as the only measure of worth.
And then there is Wegg — who takes this logic to its darkest conclusion.
Dickens gives us a passage about Wegg that I think is one of the most startling moral aphorisms in the whole novel.
'Power, unless it be the power of intellect or virtue, has ever the greatest attraction for the lowest natures.'
Wegg cannot sleep without hovering outside Boffin's house, savouring the fantasy of destruction.
That is not just character comedy — that is a portrait of what the will-to-power looks like when it has no legitimising ideology.
The image Dickens gives Wegg is almost theatrical — he is the Evil Genius of the house, and the house doesn't even know it.
'His power to strip the roof off the inhabiting family like the roof of a house of cards' — that detail of the doubled word, roof and roof, feels almost hypnotic.
And it connects, for me, to the Wegg passage where he reads out the alternative will — the one where old Harmon cuts Boffin down to the Little Mound.
Wegg reads it with such relish.
'Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him.'
That phrase — 'quite enough for him' — in a legal document.
Old Harmon even in death cannot resist the moral verdict — and Wegg reads it as his weapon.
That will document is a remarkable thing — the old man's character compressed into a single act of posthumous spite dressed as legal procedure.
And what Wegg does with it illuminates something about the moral architecture of the whole novel.
Power, as Daniel has quoted, attracts the lowest natures.
But Dickens is equally interested in what wealth does to those who receive it unexpectedly — the Boffins, the Bellas.
The great question the novel keeps posing is whether a fundamentally good person can survive sudden fortune with their goodness intact.
And Dickens, to his credit, does not give us an easy answer.
That question is exactly right — but I'd push it further.
The novel keeps showing us that the machinery surrounding wealth — the charities, the Weegs, the aristocratic form letters — doesn't care about the character of the recipient.
The postscript on that ducal letter — 'The Steward's fee is limited to three Guineas' — would read exactly the same if Boffin were the vilest man in London.
That is what the satire is actually targeting — the system that runs on gold dust regardless of the human being at its centre.
Three different angles on the same extraordinary portrait — and between them, I think, we have the full picture.
The cheese that breeds parasites; the lithographed duke; the secretive beggar on horseback; and Wegg in the dark outside the house, drunk on a power he hasn't yet spent.
Dickens is giving us the entire ecology of English wealth — not just the man who holds it, but every creature that circles around it.
Coming up, we turn to what that wealth does to Bella Wilfer — and whether Dickens finally lets her be more than a lesson.

segments.title: Close Read: The Comedy of Inconsistency—Wegg, Silas, and the Novel's Subversive Humour

utterances.text: We turn now to something that might seem, at first glance, lighter — the novel's comedy.
But Dickens's humour in Our Mutual Friend is never merely decorative.
It is, I'd argue, one of the novel's sharpest critical instruments.
Caroline Woodcourt has been sitting with some of the funniest — and most unsettling — passages in the book.
Caroline, where do you want to begin?
I want to begin with an ending — the moment Silas Wegg finally gets what's coming to him.
Because Dickens doesn't just defeat Wegg — he humiliates him with exquisite precision.
Sloppy — this enormous, button-faced, entirely underestimated young man — is given the honour.
And here is what Dickens makes of it.
"Sloppy lightly trotted out with him and trotted down the staircase, Mr Venus attending to open the street door."

"Mr Sloppy's instructions had been to deposit his burden in the road; but, a scavenger's cart happening to stand unattended at the corner, with its little ladder planted against the wheel, Mr S. found it impossible to resist the temptation of shooting Mr Silas Wegg into the cart's contents."
"A somewhat difficult feat, achieved with great dexterity, and with a prodigious splash."
"A prodigious splash." That full stop lands like a door slamming on Wegg's entire career.
What strikes me is the almost Augustan tidiness of it.
Wegg has, throughout the novel, aspired — ludicrously, grotesquely — above his station.
And the novel returns him, quite literally, to the dust heap.
But notice the weight Dickens gives Sloppy's small disobedience — the improvised shot into the cart.
He was instructed to deposit the man in the road. He does something better.
There is a moral rightness to that creative excess that Johnson himself might have approved.
I think we have to notice who is doing the throwing.
Sloppy — who was himself once an object of charity, a foundling, a non-person — physically ejects the schemer.
The novel delegates justice not to the law, not to wealth, but to the person the system had entirely written off.
That is not merely funny. That is a statement about where legitimate power actually resides.
And this moment doesn't arrive without its violent prelude — Harmon himself, earlier, grips Wegg by the cravat.
"He found himself gripped by the cravat; shaken until his teeth chattered; shoved back, staggering, into a corner of the room; and pinned there."
The comedy and the violence are not opposites here — they belong to the same corrective impulse.
Daniel's right that the violence prepares the comedy — but I want to stay with what makes that finale so purely pleasurable.
That phrase — "lightly trotted" — is doing so much work.
Sloppy doesn't lumber or struggle — he trots. Wegg is weightless to him. Weightless in every sense.
And then there's that wonderful formal hesitation before the punchline — "a scavenger's cart happening to stand unattended."
Dickens pretends it's an accident of circumstance. It is, of course, the most perfectly arranged fate imaginable.
Let's widen the frame a little, because this kind of comedy — where a character's hypocrisy is exposed mid-performance — runs right through the novel.
Caroline, you brought along a passage involving a very different sort of petty villain — the Deputy Lock.
Yes — and this one is almost unbearably compact. It's barely a paragraph, but it's a complete moral portrait.
Betty Higden — desperate, elderly, fleeing the workhouse — encounters this official, who takes her money coin by coin.
And what does he say while he pockets each one?
"I'm a man as earns his living by the sweat of his brow."
And Dickens cannot resist adding: "here he drew his sleeve across his forehead, as if this particular portion of his humble gains were the result of sheer hard labour and virtuous industry."
The gesture of wiping the non-existent sweat — Dickens staging the man's own lie for him, in real time.
It is comedy, yes. But it is also fury dressed as comedy.
I accept that the passage is savage. But I'd push back gently on the word fury.
What Dickens is anatomising here is not a system — it is a particular vice. Self-deception raised to an art form.
The Deputy Lock is not a type. He is a man who has persuaded himself that extortion is honest labour.
The comedy comes from the gap between the claim and the gesture — and that is a moral comedy, not a political one.
Edmund, with respect, those two things are not separable.
The Deputy Lock's self-deception is not a private vice — it is the ideology of petty officialdom made flesh.
Every institution in this novel — the lock, the workhouse, the counting-house — requires this kind of performance of virtue to function.
He wipes his brow because the whole system needs him to believe he deserves what he takes.
The comedy is the diagnosis, not the decoration.
That phrase — the comedy as diagnosis — brings us to what may be the novel's most audacious comic device: identity itself.
Caroline, you have a passage about John Harmon — or rather, about the vertiginous number of people John Harmon is.
This is the passage I find strangest — and most brilliant — in the whole novel.
Harmon removes his false hair and whiskers — his nautical disguise — and Dickens describes what remains.
"He ceased to be the oakum-headed, oakum-whiskered man on whom Miss Pleasant Riderhood had looked," Dickens writes.
"And became as like that same lost wanted Mr Julius Handford, as never man was like another in this world."
And then — and this is where it becomes almost giddy — he is simultaneously Rokesmith.
"For John Rokesmith, too, was as like that same lost wanted Mr Julius Handford as never man was like another in this world."
The same formula used twice in quick succession — it tips from gothic suspense into something almost comic.
Three men. One body. One sentence that keeps doubling back on itself.
What I find remarkable is the syntax — the way the repetition of that phrase enacts the instability it describes.
One does not merely read that Harmon has multiple identities — one experiences the difficulty of fixing him in a single self.
It is, in the oldest sense, a moral puzzle — who is this man, and what does he owe the world?
The comedy — if it is comedy — is the comedy of unresolvable character. Which is really tragedy wearing a light coat.
Edmund's phrase is elegant, but I think it underweights something crucial about the passage.
Harmon can only exist — can only survive — by being nobody.
The multiplication of identities is not a philosophical puzzle — it is a strategy of self-preservation against a world that would consume him for his inheritance.
That the passage feels comic — vertiginous, as the host put it — is because Dickens understands that self-erasure, under capitalism, is both absurd and entirely rational.
Three identities, a scavenger's cart, a man wiping imaginary sweat from his brow — and in all of it, the same underlying intelligence at work.
The comedy and the critique are, in Dickens, genuinely inseparable — which is perhaps what makes him so difficult to put down, and so rewarding to return to.
Our thanks to Caroline, Daniel, and Edmund for a close read that has been anything but light.

segments.title: Discussion: Money, Meaning, and the Self—What Our Mutual Friend Still Demands

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've spent time in the dust-heaps and on the river, with the Veneerings and the Lammles and the whole gilded pageant of nouveau-riche London.
But today we're going deeper — into the novel's most intimate and perhaps most troubling question.
What does money do to the self — to identity, to love, to the possibility of redemption?
To explore that, I'm joined by three people who know this novel with quite extraordinary depth.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — he'll want to know exactly whose interests a deception serves.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who insists the novel is finally a story about moral character — about whether goodness is possible under pressure.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and close reader who trusts what the prose actually does on the page — and who has re-read this novel more times than she cares to count.
Let's begin with John Harmon — or Rokesmith, or whatever name we choose to give him.
Because this man chooses to remain dead — and the novel asks us to decide whether that choice is noble or monstrous.
What strikes me every time I return to these chapters is the sheer strangeness of what Harmon is doing.
He is lying in a public-house bed, having nearly been murdered, and instead of simply going to the authorities — he begins to plot.
Dickens gives us the precise moment the idea crystallises, and he gives it to us in Harmon's own words.
'the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella'
'Proving Bella.' There is something almost forensic about that phrase — and something deeply uncomfortable.
He's treating a woman's character as a hypothesis to be tested rather than a person to be known.
And yet — Dickens makes it almost tender, too.
I think we need to be precise about what that tenderness is covering over.
Harmon is an heir — a man of enormous inherited wealth — who sets himself up as a judge of an impoverished woman's virtue.
The power differential there is not incidental — it is the entire structure of the situation.
And the novel is honest about where this comes from.

'When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless.'
'Never yet for good.' That is the key phrase.
The father's money has never produced anything but damage — and yet the son still inherits it, still exercises its power, still tests Bella from a position of total informational advantage.
The deception may be psychologically comprehensible — but it is also an act of class domination, dressed up as romantic scruple.
Daniel makes the structural case with his customary vigour, and I shan't dismiss it entirely.
But the passage he quotes is doing something rather more subtle than a diagram of power.
Harmon is trapped — genuinely, existentially trapped — in an impossible dilemma of his own partial making and his father's full making.
The novel spells it out with unusual directness.
'Was it for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?'
That is a moral question of genuine anguish — not a political one.
The father's will has created conditions under which every choice available to Harmon involves a corruption of his own integrity.
That is what Dickens is exploring — the moral weight of inherited circumstance on a man who is trying, however clumsily, to be good.
Edmund, I want to come back to something — because the deception didn't begin with Harmon alone.
There's an earlier moment, on the boat, where we see how the whole scheme was hatched with Radfoot — this stranger Harmon befriended, who would later try to murder him.
And the way Dickens writes it, you feel the seductive ease of the plan — how it seemed so harmless, so reasonable.
Here is how the scheme is described:

'the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses (as he was able to guide me about London), and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way'
'Common sailors' dresses' — the heir of a fortune, playing poor, watching a poor woman.
There is something almost farcical about it — and something that makes you quite uneasy on Bella's behalf.
That farcicality is doing real work, though.
Class disguise is one of Dickens's great satirical instruments throughout the novel — and it cuts in every direction.
The rich pretend to be poor; the newly rich pretend to be grand.
And what about the institutions of charity — the magnificent Patronesses and Vice-Patronesses that Boffin so magnificently demolishes?
Boffin's rant about charitable giving is one of the most precise dissections of bourgeois philanthropy I know in Victorian fiction.

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
The accumulation of titles is not ornamental — it enacts the very proliferation of vanity it mocks.
Five shillings buys you the title of Patron — and that title is the real transaction, not the charity itself.
On that, I find myself entirely with Daniel — which ought perhaps to alarm us both.
Boffin's comedy here is not merely satirical — it is the voice of plain sense against institutional pretension.
'If it ain't stark staring impudence, what do you call it?' — one can't improve on that.
What interests me is that Boffin — the dust-heap heir, the self-made man — is the one who sees through the performance.
Not the educated, not the aristocratic — but the man who came to money late and has not yet learned to be deceived by its ornaments.
And that's why I think Boffin is, in a strange way, the novel's moral compass — at least in these chapters.
Because he's not performing goodness — he simply is good, without the apparatus of charity titles and social credit.
Which is exactly the contrast Dickens needs when he shows us Harmon's elaborate machinery of 'proving' Bella.
The novel keeps asking: can goodness survive wealth?
Can love survive being turned into a test?
And those questions have lost precisely none of their force since 1865.
The machinery of philanthropy as reputation-laundering; the heir who tests the woman he already has power over; the deception that was meant to last only a few hours.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel that knows exactly what money costs — not just in pounds, but in selfhood.
Daniel, Edmund, Caroline — thank you for an extraordinary conversation.
We'll be back shortly to take the discussion further.

segments.title: Closing: The River and the Ashes—Renewal, Redemption, and the Limits of Reform

utterances.text: We've reached the end of our journey through Our Mutual Friend — a novel that began with a body dragged from the Thames and ends, somehow, in something like grace.
This closing segment asks the largest question the novel poses: what, if anything, survives the dust heaps?
Is there genuine renewal here — moral, social, personal — or does Dickens offer us a redemption that the novel's own evidence quietly undermines?
Edmund, I want to begin with you — because you've been arguing all episode that the novel's moral imagination is its truest achievement.
There's a passage about old John Harmon — the dead miser — that I think speaks directly to what you mean.
Yes — and it's a passage that rewards very careful attention, because Dickens is doing something quietly extraordinary here.
Old Harmon is, by any accounting, a monstrous figure — a man who weaponised his wealth against everyone he touched.
And yet the narrator tells us that even through his most inveterate purposes, something in him recognised genuine virtue — and could not corrupt it.
The narrator gives us a sentence of almost Johnsonian precision on this point.
"he had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt"
The powerlessness of all his wealth — that is the novel's central moral claim, stated with the quiet authority of a verdict.
Goodness, Dickens insists, cannot be purchased — and a man who knows this, even if he cannot live by it, has not entirely lost his humanity.
Edmund, I admire the reading — but I think it lets the novel off a very important hook.
Old Harmon's recognition of the Boffins' virtue doesn't redeem the system that made him what he was.
He wrote their names in his will — fine — but the wealth he accumulated through decades of exploitation is still the engine that drives every plot in the novel.
Recognising that goodness can't be bought is not the same as dismantling the buying-and-selling that structures every relationship in this world.
The dust heaps are dispersed — but they're dispersed among the same class of people who already held property.
You're right, of course, that Dickens doesn't redesign the economy — but I'm not sure he ever claimed to.
His quarrel is with what money does to individual souls — and on that ground he prosecutes his case with extraordinary rigour.
Consider Bradley Headstone — a man destroyed not by poverty but by a refusal of conscience.
The narrator gives us this portrait of psychological damnation that I find genuinely harrowing.
"He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently."
There is no social programme that reaches this — no redistribution of wealth that heals what Headstone has become.
This is Dickens as moralist, and he is at his most penetrating.
What strikes me about that Headstone passage — and I've read it many times — is the word 'incessantly.'
He doesn't just repeat the deed in his mind — he rehearses improvements.
He is perfecting his crime forever, in a private hell of craft — and that is so much more terrible than simple guilt.
But what I keep coming back to is the contrast — because the novel holds this darkness right alongside passages of almost unbearable lightness.
The supper scene with Bella and John Rokesmith and her father — it's so slight, so domestic, and yet it moved me the first time I read it and it still does.
Listen to how Dickens writes it — the fairy-tale register is deliberate, and it's doing real work.

"It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, 'Somebody's been drinking my milk!'"
'Without their thunderous low growlings' — that's the whole novel in one clause, isn't it?
Joy is defined here as the absence of threat — happiness as the fairy tale that, just this once, turns out safe.
Caroline, I hear that — and I don't want to trample on it.
But notice where this meal takes place — in the offices of Chicksey, Veneering, and Stobbles, with the iron safe staring at them like a dull dragon.
Dickens himself names it — the iron safe, the dull dragon of capital — even in the scene of greatest domestic happiness.
The novel cannot quite imagine joy without also imaging the system that constrains it — and that, to my mind, is Dickens thinking more clearly than his sentimentalism would like.
I think that's exactly right — and it's why the passage works.
The 'uncongenial oddity of its surroundings' — Dickens puts that phrase in, and it makes the happiness more precarious, and therefore more precious.
These people are happy inside the machine — briefly, tenderly, against all odds.
I find I can agree with both of you, and I'm not sure that constitutes a contradiction.
Dickens is a novelist, not a pamphleteer — his power comes precisely from holding darkness and light in the same sentence, sometimes in the same clause.
The Headstone portrait and the hobgoblin supper are not contradictions — they are the full range of what the novel claims human life can be.
And that old miser, scratching two faithful names into his will — that too is part of the range.
Even the worst of men, Dickens insists, can dimly perceive goodness — even if he cannot choose it.
And perhaps that is where we must leave Our Mutual Friend — with that unresolved, irreducible tension.
A novel that shows us the worst the Thames can dredge up — and then, in the same current, floats a fairy-tale supper and a miser's grudging act of faith.
My warmest thanks to Daniel Rosen, Edmund Leigh, and Caroline Woodcourt — three readers whose disagreements have been as illuminating as their agreements.
This has been Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.

c44:p10.text:
The haggard head floated up the dark staircase, and softly descended
      nearer to the floor outside the outer door of the chambers. The doors of
      the rooms within, appeared to be standing open. There were rays of
      candlelight from one of them, and there was the sound of a footstep going
      about. There were two voices. The words they uttered were not
      distinguishable, but they were both the voices of men. In a few moments
      the voices were silent, and there was no sound of footstep, and the inner
      light went out. If Lightwood could have seen the face which kept him
      awake, staring and listening in the darkness outside the door as he spoke
      of it, he might have been less disposed to sleep, through the remainder of
      the night.
c44:p10.summary: Bradley creeps up the dark staircase to listen outside the chambers where Wrayburn and Lightwood are present. After hearing two male voices and candlelight, the voices cease and the light goes out. An omniscient narrator warns that had Lightwood seen Bradley's face watching from the darkness, he would have been even more disturbed.
c44:p10.best_quote: If Lightwood could have seen the face which kept him awake, staring and listening in the darkness outside the door as he spoke of it, he might have been less disposed to sleep, through the remainder of the night.

c52:p102.text:
She passed out and he followed her. Mr and Mrs Boffin had the curiosity
      softly to raise a window and look after them as they went down the long
      street. They walked arm-in-arm, showily enough, but without appearing to
      interchange a syllable. It might have been fanciful to suppose that under
      their outer bearing there was something of the shamed air of two cheats
      who were linked together by concealed handcuffs; but, not so, to suppose
      that they were haggardly weary of one another, of themselves, and of all
      this world. In turning the street corner they might have turned out of
      this world, for anything Mr and Mrs Boffin ever saw of them to the
      contrary; for, they set eyes on the Lammles never more.
c52:p102.summary: The Lammles depart arm-in-arm but in silence and spiritual wretchedness, walking with all the appearance of propriety but no genuine connection, and are never seen again—Dickens' final judgment on their morally empty lives.
c52:p102.best_quote: In turning the street corner they might have turned out of this world, for anything Mr and Mrs Boffin ever saw of them to the contrary

c28:p107.text:
It being Lizzie’s regular occupation when they were alone of an evening to
      brush out and smooth the long fair hair of the dolls’ dressmaker, she
      unfastened a ribbon that kept it back while the little creature was at her
      work, and it fell in a beautiful shower over the poor shoulders that were
      much in need of such adorning rain. ‘Not now, Lizzie, dear,’ said Jenny;
      ‘let us have a talk by the fire.’ With those words, she in her turn
      loosened her friend’s dark hair, and it dropped of its own weight over her
      bosom, in two rich masses. Pretending to compare the colours and admire
      the contrast, Jenny so managed a mere touch or two of her nimble hands, as
      that she herself laying a cheek on one of the dark folds, seemed blinded
      by her own clustering curls to all but the fire, while the fine handsome
      face and brow of Lizzie were revealed without obstruction in the sombre
      light.
c28:p107.summary: Lizzie offers to brush and smooth Miss Wren's long fair hair as they prepare for an evening talk by the fire, then Miss Wren loosens Lizzie's dark hair, creating a tender scene of mutual care and contrasting beauty.
c28:p107.best_quote: it fell in a beautiful shower over the poor shoulders that were much in need of such adorning rain.

c38:p47.text:
‘Not a bit, my dear,’ said Mr Boffin. ‘But I think it’s very creditable in
      you, at your age, to be so well up with the pace of the world, and to know
      what to go in for. You are right. Go in for money, my love. Money’s the
      article. You’ll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin
      and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you’ll live and
      die rich. That’s the state to live and die in!’ said Mr Boffin, in an
      unctuous manner. ‘R—r—rich!’
c38:p47.summary: Mr Boffin emphatically advises Bella to pursue money above all else, declaring that she should capitalize on her beauty and the wealth they will bestow on her to become and remain rich.
c38:p47.best_quote: Go in for money, my love. Money's the article. You'll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you'll live and die rich.

c38:p55.text:
Somehow, Bella was not so well pleased with this assurance and this
      prospect as she might have been. Somehow, when she put her arms round Mrs
      Boffin’s neck and said Good Night, she derived a sense of unworthiness
      from the still anxious face of that good woman and her obvious wish to
      excuse her husband. ‘Why, what need to excuse him?’ thought Bella, sitting
      down in her own room. ‘What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very
      true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don’t I like it
      then? No, I don’t like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I
      disparage him for it. Then pray,’ said Bella, sternly putting the question
      to herself in the looking-glass as usual, ‘what do you mean by this, you
      inconsistent little Beast?’
c38:p55.summary: Alone in her room, Bella grapples with her confused reaction to Mr Boffin's advice: she finds his sentiments sensible and true to her own desires, yet she is repelled by them and finds herself disparaging him for expressing them, finally questioning herself severely in the mirror.
c38:p55.best_quote: Why, what need to excuse him? What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it. Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?

c42:p156.text:
The question was so directly at variance with Bella’s views in life, as
      set forth to her father, that she said internally, ‘There, you little
      mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain’t you ashamed of your self?’ and
      unclasped the girdle of her arms, expressly to give herself a penitential
      poke in the side.
c42:p156.summary: Bella experiences an internal moment of shame at her own mercenary values when confronted by Lizzie's selfless love, and literally punishes herself with a poke in the side.
c42:p156.best_quote: There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of your self?

c42:p162.text:
‘It was late upon a wretched night,’ said Lizzie, ‘when his eyes first
      looked at me in my old river-side home, very different from this. His eyes
      may never look at me again. I would rather that they never did; I hope
      that they never may. But I would not have the light of them taken out of
      my life, for anything my life can give me. I have told you everything now,
      my dear. If it comes a little strange to me to have parted with it, I am
      not sorry. I had no thought of ever parting with a single word of it, a
      moment before you came in; but you came in, and my mind changed.’
c42:p162.summary: Lizzie recalls the rainy night she first met Eugene and confesses that sharing her feelings with Bella has been healing, though unexpected.
c42:p162.best_quote: I would not have the light of them taken out of my life, for anything my life can give me.

c31:p125.text:
The Secretary looked on from a doorway at the boofer lady thus encircled,
      and still looked on at the boofer lady standing alone there, when the
      determined old figure with its steady bright eyes was trudging through the
      streets, away from paralysis and pauperism.
c31:p125.summary: Rokesmith watches from a doorway as Betty departs with steady determination, then observes Bella standing alone—a moment that captures his emotional detachment and the poignancy of their separation.
c31:p125.best_quote: The Secretary looked on from a doorway at the boofer lady thus encircled, and still looked on at the boofer lady standing alone there, when the determined old figure with its steady bright eyes was trudging through the streets, away from paralysis and pauperism.

c38:p42.text:
Bella ventured for a moment to look stealthily towards him under her
      eyelashes, and she saw a dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and
      conceit, overshadowing the once open face.
c38:p42.summary: Bella observes a dark expression of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit shadowing Mr Boffin's formerly open countenance.
c38:p42.best_quote: A dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit, overshadowing the once open face.

c8:p39.text:
‘And speaking of satisfactory,’ pursued Mr Boffin, ‘why, Lord save us!
      when we come to take it to pieces, bit by bit, where’s the
      satisfactoriness of the money as yet? When the old man does right the poor
      boy after all, the poor boy gets no good of it. He gets made away with, at
      the moment when he’s lifting (as one may say) the cup and sarser to his
      lips. Mr Lightwood, I will now name to you, that on behalf of the poor
      dear boy, me and Mrs Boffin have stood out against the old man times out
      of number, till he has called us every name he could lay his tongue to. I
      have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the
      claims of the nat’ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin’s bonnet (she wore,
      in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top
      of her head), and send it spinning across the yard. I have indeed. And
      once, when he did this in a manner that amounted to personal, I should
      have given him a rattler for himself, if Mrs Boffin hadn’t thrown herself
      betwixt us, and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr
      Lightwood. Dropped her.’
c8:p39.summary: Boffin details how he and Mrs Boffin repeatedly defended young John Harmon against Old Harmon's cruelty, including an incident where Harmon struck Mrs Boffin and she collapsed, establishing their selfless advocacy for the boy.
c8:p39.best_quote: I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet (she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head), and send it spinning across the yard... and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.

c9:p23.text:
Mrs Boffin pulled his nearest ear, in acknowledgment of this piece of
      philosophy, and then said, gradually toning down to a motherly strain:
      ‘Last, and not least, I have taken a fancy. You remember dear little John
      Harmon, before he went to school? Over yonder across the yard, at our
      fire? Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it’s come to us, I
      should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and
      give him John’s name, and provide for him. Somehow, it would make me
      easier, I fancy. Say it’s only a whim—’
c9:p23.summary: Mrs Boffin proposes adopting an orphan child, naming him John Harmon in memory of the young heir who drowned, thereby using their inherited fortune for redemptive good.
c9:p23.best_quote: Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him.

c64:p95.text:
‘I mean to knock your head against the wall,’ returned John Harmon,
      suiting his action to his words, with the heartiest good will; ‘and I’d
      give a thousand pounds for leave to knock your brains out. Listen, you
      scoundrel, and look at that Dutch bottle.’
c64:p95.summary: Harmon violently interrogates Wegg while ordering Sloppy to hold up the Dutch bottle, explaining its significance and his own indebtedness to Boffin.
c64:p95.best_quote: and I'd give a thousand pounds for leave to knock your brains out.

c64:p97.text:
‘That Dutch bottle, scoundrel, contained the latest will of the many wills
      made by my unhappy self-tormenting father. That will gives everything
      absolutely to my noble benefactor and yours, Mr Boffin, excluding and
      reviling me, and my sister (then already dead of a broken heart), by name.
      That Dutch bottle was found by my noble benefactor and yours, after he
      entered on possession of the estate. That Dutch bottle distressed him
      beyond measure, because, though I and my sister were both no more, it cast
      a slur upon our memory which he knew we had done nothing in our miserable
      youth, to deserve. That Dutch bottle, therefore, he buried in the Mound
      belonging to him, and there it lay while you, you thankless wretch, were
      prodding and poking—often very near it, I dare say. His intention
      was, that it should never see the light; but he was afraid to destroy it,
      lest to destroy such a document, even with his great generous motive,
      might be an offence at law. After the discovery was made here who I was,
      Mr Boffin, still restless on the subject, told me, upon certain conditions
      impossible for such a hound as you to appreciate, the secret of that Dutch
      bottle. I urged upon him the necessity of its being dug up, and the paper
      being legally produced and established. The first thing you saw him do,
      and the second thing has been done without your knowledge. Consequently,
      the paper now rattling in your hand as I shake you—and I should like
      to shake the life out of you—is worth less than the rotten cork of
      the Dutch bottle, do you understand?’
c64:p97.summary: Harmon explains how the Dutch bottle was found by Boffin after entering the estate, buried in the Mound to hide its contents, and later exhumed without Wegg's knowledge.
c64:p97.best_quote: That Dutch bottle, scoundrel, contained the latest will of the many wills made by my unhappy self-tormenting father. c64:p99.text:
‘Now, scoundrel,’ said John Harmon, taking another sailor-like turn on his
      cravat and holding him in his corner at arms’ length, ‘I shall make two
      more short speeches to you, because I hope they will torment you. Your
      discovery was a genuine discovery (such as it was), for nobody had thought
      of looking into that place. Neither did we know you had made it, until
      Venus spoke to Mr Boffin, though I kept you under good observation from my
      first appearance here, and though Sloppy has long made it the chief
      occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow. I tell
      you this, that you may know we knew enough of you to persuade Mr Boffin to
      let us lead you on, deluded, to the last possible moment, in order that
      your disappointment might be the heaviest possible disappointment. That’s
      the first short speech, do you understand?’

c25:p0.text:
The minion of fortune and the worm of the hour, or in less cutting
      language, Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, the Golden Dustman, had become as
      much at home in his eminently aristocratic family mansion as he was likely
      ever to be. He could not but feel that, like an eminently aristocratic
      family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite
      amount of parasites; but he was content to regard this drawback on his
      property as a sort of perpetual Legacy Duty. He felt the more resigned to
      it, forasmuch as Mrs Boffin enjoyed herself completely, and Miss Bella was
      delighted.
c25:p0.summary: Nicodemus Boffin, the newly wealthy Golden Dustman, has settled into his grand mansion, finding it oversized but content because Mrs Boffin and Bella are delighted.

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.
c17:p5.best_quote: they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf

c40:p97.text:
For, Silas Wegg felt it to be quite out of the question that he could lay
      his head upon his pillow in peace, without first hovering over Mr Boffin’s
      house in the superior character of its Evil Genius. Power (unless it be
      the power of intellect or virtue) has ever the greatest attraction for the
      lowest natures; and the mere defiance of the unconscious house-front, with
      his power to strip the roof off the inhabiting family like the roof of a
      house of cards, was a treat which had a charm for Silas Wegg.
c40:p97.summary: Wegg cannot rest without hovering over Boffin's house, fantasizing about his power to destroy it, demonstrating how power appeals to base natures.
c40:p97.best_quote: Power (unless it be the power of intellect or virtue) has ever the greatest attraction for the lowest natures; and the mere defiance of the unconscious house-front, with his power to strip the roof off the inhabiting family like the roof of a house of cards, was a treat which had a charm for Silas Wegg.

c40:p31.text:
‘Exactly so, sir!’ returned Wegg, blandly and buoyantly. ‘I see I take you
      with me! Hear, hear, hear! Resolved, as your discriminating good sense
      perceives, that if you was to have a sap—pur— ize , it should be
      a complete one! Well, sir. And so, as you have honoured me by
      anticipating, I examined the document. Regularly executed, regularly
      witnessed, very short. Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever
      had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the
      Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and
      residue of his property to the Crown.’

c64:p118.text:
The words were but out of his mouth when John Harmon lifted his finger,
      and Sloppy, who was now close to Wegg, backed to Wegg’s back, stooped,
      grasped his coat collar behind with both hands, and deftly swung him up
      like the sack of flour or coals before mentioned. A countenance of special
      discontent and amazement Mr Wegg exhibited in this position, with his
      buttons almost as prominently on view as Sloppy’s own, and with his wooden
      leg in a highly unaccommodating state. But, not for many seconds was his
      countenance visible in the room; for, Sloppy lightly trotted out with him
      and trotted down the staircase, Mr Venus attending to open the street
      door. Mr Sloppy’s instructions had been to deposit his burden in the road;
      but, a scavenger’s cart happening to stand unattended at the corner, with
      its little ladder planted against the wheel, Mr S. found it impossible to
      resist the temptation of shooting Mr Silas Wegg into the cart’s contents.
      A somewhat difficult feat, achieved with great dexterity, and with a
      prodigious splash.

Wegg had repeated the word with a sneer, and was entering on some

c41:p60.text:
‘I’m a man,’ said the Deputy, giving her back the letter, and pocketing
      the coins, one by one, ‘as earns his living by the sweat of his brow;’
      here he drew his sleeve across his forehead, as if this particular portion
      of his humble gains were the result of sheer hard labour and virtuous
      industry; ‘and I won’t stand in your way. Go where you like.’
